name: Cocklebur (Xanthium, Xanthii Fructus)
short: Poisoning: a man died of multi-organ failure after 2 months of unprocessed cocklebur fruit for rhinitis; liver transplant (title only); 19 of 76 died in an outbreak attributed to eating seedlings.
text: Poisoning and death (case reports and series): a 55-year-old man with allergic rhinitis who took unprocessed cocklebur fruit (Xanthii Fructus) for 2 months as treatment developed loss of appetite, nausea, abdominal pain, very low urine output, sharply raised liver enzymes and creatinine, and clotting abnormalities, and died of worsening multiple organ failure despite dialysis; the authors state that serious poisoning can easily occur with overdose, improper processing or use without processing. A 17-year-old who was prescribed a pill preparation derived from Xanthium sibiricum for chronic allergies developed intermittent muscle spasms of the face, neck and arms shortly after her second dose, which eased over 4 days after she stopped; testing of the product found no other medicines or drugs, and the authors note 11 described cases of accidental human ingestion of Xanthium leading to spasm, somnolence, low blood sugar, and kidney and liver toxicity. Nine people were poisoned by carboxyatractyloside, the toxin in cocklebur seeds, with abdominal pain, vomiting, drowsiness and breathlessness; three had convulsions and died within 48 hours, and post-mortem examination showed liver necrosis and kidney tubule necrosis (the abstract does not say what was eaten or why). Liver transplantation: a case report is titled 'Xanthium strumarium poisoning requiring liver transplantation'; the record has no abstract, so the patient, the product and how it was taken cannot be reported. A review of liver injury from traditional Chinese medicine lists Cang Er Zi among the herbal products with potential liver toxicity in reported cases (the abstract does not give its plant source; the pill in the 17-year-old's case, Cang Er Zi Wan, is described as derived from Xanthium sibiricum), and says that for some patients the course was severe, with risks of acute liver failure, liver transplantation and death; the abstract does not say which products these patients had taken, and notes that the case data were affected by adulteration, contamination with heavy metals and misidentification. In a 2007 outbreak in Bangladesh after floods, 76 people became ill and 19 (25%) died; 31 of 33 cases interviewed had eaten cocklebur seedlings in the hours before falling ill, eaten as a main meal because other food was unavailable, and people who ate the plant were 34.2 times more likely to develop vomiting and unconsciousness; vomiting, raised liver enzymes and altered consciousness were common, and the authors conclude that eating the seedlings in large quantities, because other food was unavailable, caused the outbreak. These seedling and seed data concern the plant eaten as food or by accident, not a prepared medicine. Reviews of Xanthii Fructus as a medicine name liver and kidney injury as the main side effects, with nerve and heart toxicity also common, report skin reactions up to exfoliative dermatitis after use by mouth or on the skin, and say poisoning occurs with excessive use, use without preparation or inappropriate preparation. On the other side, a meta-analysis of 15 trials (1361 children with allergic rhinitis) of the multi-herb Chinese formula Cang-Er-Zi-San (the abstract does not list its ingredients) reported adverse events as better in the formula group than with other therapies, without giving figures, and the authors note biased results and limited research. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
